articles.title: U.S. Ally Warns It Can No Longer Trust Trump’s America
articles.description: One of our closest allies now believes that it can’t rely on the United States under President Donald Trump’s leadership. Belgium’s foreign ministry warned that America was “no longer the ally it has been in the past,” according to a late-2025 strategy document reviewed by the Financial Times . The Belgian document called for a “thorough re-evaluation of the relation between the European Union and Belgium on the one hand, and the U.S. on the other hand.” It argued that the current political dynamics in the United States were “likely to compromise several vital interests of Belgium and the European Union. The document maintained that engagement with the Trump administration was “indispensable,” but also acknowledged that it was mostly a lost cause. The document advised that a dialogue with levels below the federal government should be “significantly reinforced,” that discussions should be held with Democratic opposition, and that Belgian officials should focus on “identifying the new generations of bipartisan elites that could play a role in tomorrow’s America.” The document was produced around the same time that the Trump administration issued its controversial 2025 National Security Strategy , which showed a clear ideological shift to implicitly condemn centrist and liberal governments in Europe, and boost the right-wing groups that opposed them, warning them to curb immigration or risk “civilizational erasure.” Simultaneously, the Trump administration continued in its unwanted advances to acquire Greenland from Denmark, while flubbing its proposed peace deal between Russia and Ukraine. Clearly, European countries would be right to be concerned: since then, the president has continued issuing threats to pull U.S. forces out of Europe altogether.

articles.title: A strong El Niño actually means fewer Atlantic hurricanes, but the Pacific has been extra stormy
articles.description: The Atlantic Ocean has had an unusually quiet hurricane season this year. Though there have been six named storms , zero have actually strengthened into hurricanes—a rarity that hasn’t occurred in decades. On the other side of the country, though, Hurricane Polo has rapidly intensified, becoming one of the most intense East Pacific hurricanes on record. These weather anomalies may seem at odds, but they’re both impacted by the “ Godzilla ” Super El Niño that experts say is shaping up to be one of the strongest in history. El Niño affects weather patterns around the world, and can amplify extreme weather events. And even though El Niño may reduce the number of hurricanes in the Atlantic, that doesn’t always mean the season is less destructive than other years. It’s late September—where are all the Atlantic hurricanes? The Atlantic hurricane season spans from June 1 to November 30, though the season tends to peak around September 10, making it unusual, AccuWeather notes, “not to have a hurricane spinning on that date.” On average, a season sees 14 named storms in the Atlantic, with seven that become hurricanes and three that strengthen into major hurricanes. By September 24 this year, though, there have still been no hurricanes in that ocean. (Tropical Storm Fay is spinning in the central Atlantic Ocean, but it poses no threat to the United States, experts say.) “The latest occurrence of the first Atlantic hurricane in the last 100 years was September 21, 1941,” Chad Merrill, a senior meteorologist with AccuWeather, tells Fast Company. “That record is being demolished as we speak.” “In the entire record of the Atlantic basin, the latest occurrence of the first hurricane was October 7, 1905. It’s yet to be seen if this record is demolished,” he adds. Hurricanes need three features to form, the U.S. Geological Survey notes: warm ocean water; warm air at the ocean’s surface that can then cool and rise; and “low wind shear,” or little difference in the wind’s speed and direction within different levels of the atmosphere. A predominant feature of an El Niño is hotter ocean water in the Pacific. But the phenomenon still affects activity in the Atlantic, too. There’s less of a chance of Atlantic hurricanes during El Niño years because of the way it changes winds: increased wind shear means stronger winds sweeping across the Atlantic, which makes it less likely for storms to form and strengthen. El Niño fuels more hurricanes in the Pacific Across the country, hurricane season looks starkly different. There have already been 16 named storms and six hurricanes that have formed across the Central and Eastern Pacific, fueled by El Niño’s warmer waters and lower wind shear there. Typically, an El Niño means drier-than-normal conditions in the northeastern parts of the U.S., and wetter-than-normal conditions across the south. El Niños also strengthen the Pacific jet stream, a current of air that flows from west to east. That stronger jet stream, combined with the hot Pacific ocean temperatures, can strengthen storms that hit the west coast of the country. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) predicted that the Pacific hurricane season would be above average, with 9-14 hurricanes and 5-9 major hurricanes in that ocean, fueled by this record-breaking El Niño. The latest example of this effect is Hurricane Polo, a Category 4 storm off the southwest coast of Mexico that meteorologists have said is one of the strongest Pacific basin storms on record. Though that storm is off the coast of Mexico, the strong jet stream could draw moisture north bringing a “good chance” of flash flooding to New Mexico, Texas, and Oklahoma, Merrill says. Experts are also warning that Tropical Storm Nolo in the Pacific could soon be a major hurricane, potentially bringing more than 30 inches of extreme rain to Hawaii’s Big Island. Super El Niño means all sorts of extreme weather Though this year’s El Niño may mean fewer Atlantic hurricanes, that doesn’t mean anyone is completely safe from the weather phenomenon’s impacts. El Niño is a natural phenomenon, but this year’s warm ocean temperatures of El Niño are combining with already record-breakingly hot oceans due to climate change, creating a “Godzilla Super El Niño” that is particularly strong. It’s not that climate change is directly making the El Niño stronger, climatologist Michael Mann told BCC, but “it’s like a wave that’s on top of a rising tide . . . Every time we get a large El Niño event like this one, it’s sitting on top of a warmer planet.” That warmth on top of warmth can supercharge extreme weather everywhere. “When the oceans are warmer, thanks to climate change and the developing El Niño, they release vast amounts of moisture into the atmosphere, which act as extra fuel for any storm,” Union of Concerned Scientists climate scientist Marc Alessi wrote on BlueSky. That’s evident through Tropical Storm Nolo, which is being fueled by record ocean heat—as well as an early-season Nor’easter developing in the Atlantic, he adds, and the extreme rain in New Mexico. El Niño could also bring sharp cold fronts into the Great Lakes and Northeast, Merrill notes, and even warm and dry weather to the West, which leads to a higher-than-average fire risk. In this way, this record-breaking El Niño could be a glimpse into our future , where a warmer world fuels extreme weather that affects the entire planet, in one way or another.

articles.title: Tajikistan Developing a National Framework on Disaster Risk Data Governance
articles.description: Country: Tajikistan Source: UN Office for Disaster Risk Reduction On 16-17 September 2026, the Committee of Emergency Situations and Civil Defence, with the support of the Asian and Pacific Centre for the Development of Disaster Information Management (ESCAP-APDIM) and the United Nations Office for Disaster Risk Reduction (UNDRR), held a multi-stakeholder consultation workshop on the development of a National Framework for Inclusive Disaster Risk Data Governance. The event brought together representatives of ministries and government agencies, development partners, and international organizations. The main objective of the workshop was to strengthen inter-agency cooperation and improve mechanisms for the collection, sharing, and management of disaster risk data including the development of a National Framework for Inclusive Disaster Risk Data Governance. The workshop also contributed to further expanding the ongoing collaboration of the Committee with ESCAP-APDIM, UNDRR, the Government of Switzerland and other partners, to strengthen disaster risk information governance and management in Tajikistan. Deputy Chairman of the Committee, Major General Muhabbat Ibrohimzoda, emphasized in his remarks that establishing a unified and integrated data management system is essential for accurate risk assessment, timely decision-making, the planning of preventive measures, and the development of effective early warning systems. Ms. Parvathy Ramaswami, the UN Resident Coordinator in Tajikistan highlighted that “Tajikistan can ensure that reliable data is collected, analyzed, and consistently drives decisions. Effective disaster risk management depends on knowing where risks are emerging, who is most exposed and vulnerable, how conditions are changing, and where action and resources are needed the most.” Mr. Mostafa Mohaghegh, Senior Coordinator of ESCAP-APDIM commended Tajikistan’s achievements in disaster risk reduction and information management and stressed the critical role of disaster risk data governance to ensure tangible and measurable results and impacts in disaster risk reduction and management. He emphasized the significance of the National Framework for Inclusive Disaster Risk Data Governance and sharing Tajikistan’s valuable experience in this regard with the other countries of the region. Mr. Dilshod Kodirov, Programme Management Officer at UNDRR, noted that the process should build on existing systems and initiatives, with the objective of establishing a practical framework that connects existing efforts and helps turn disaster risk information into action. The workshop reviewed the existing DRR legal and institutional frameworks in Tajikistan and addressed key issues related to inter-agency coordination, data analysis, sharing and integration, interoperability of information systems, disaster loss and damage accounting, as well as the application of the DELTA Resilience system. Particular attention was given to the discussion of the draft National Framework for Inclusive Disaster Risk Data Governance in the Republic of Tajikistan. Participants identified existing challenges, priority areas, and further steps towards establishing an effective and coordinated disaster risk data governance and management system. The outcomes of the workshop provide a solid basis for the further refinement of the National Framework and Roadmap, improved data collection, analysis and exchange among relevant institutions, and stronger inter-agency cooperation in the field of disaster risk reduction contributing to the achievement of Sustainable Development Goals in Tajikistan.

articles.title: Successful woodland expansion in Scotland’s Cairngorms revealed in aerial maps
articles.description: Successful woodland expansion in Scotland’s Cairngorms revealed in aerial maps Jacqueline Garget Thu, 09/24/2026 - 05:01 A University of Cambridge-led team has used aerial surveys across a huge swathe of the Cairngorms National Park in Scotland to create detailed 3D maps that show the beginnings of large-scale recovery of native woodland. The maps document a success-story for the Cairngorms Connect nature restoration partnership: young trees are spreading naturally into areas where woodlands have been missing for centuries, following a landscape-scale approach to deer management across the partnership’s 60,000 hectares. From a light aircraft flown 600m above the ground, a laser scanning technology known as LiDAR collected the data used by the Cambridge team. Their new, AI-supported method of analysing the data revealed over six million individual trees across the 569km 2 survey area, as well as the exact height of every tree. The results show that 2.65 million trees - just over 40% of those surveyed - were under five metres tall. These small, regenerating trees grow mostly near the edges of existing forests, where seeds are most likely to fall - but some new trees were found growing over half a kilometre from the forest edge. The maps also show that habitat type matters for tree regeneration: fewer new trees had established in boggy areas than in dry heathlands. “The ability to map regenerating trees so precisely, at such a huge scale, is a breakthrough for monitoring nature restoration at a landscape scale. It means we can effectively map young trees, assess whether restoration targets are being met, and inform future restoration work,” said Dr Aland Chan in the University of Cambridge’s Centre for Landscape Regeneration, who co-led the work. “The new LiDAR-based method is excellent at tracking where new woodlands are establishing across the landscape, and also for tracking the impacts of fires - which are increasing in severity with climate change,” said Dr Pip Gullett from the Cairngorms Connect partnership, co-author of the study. She added: “This is going to be a great way to monitor large-scale woodland expansion going forward, as more and more landowners across Scotland are looking to re-establish native woodlands.” The study is published today in the Journal of Applied Ecology . Airborne LiDAR shoots laser beams at high frequency from a light aircraft towards the ground, which bounce back when they hit trees or any other surface. By recording the time taken for each laser pulse to bounce back to the plane, the team could create a three-dimensional image of the landscape with vastly more detail than is possible to collect through ground-based surveys. Point measurements on the ground validated the accuracy of the results, and comparison with field surveys conducted by Cairngorms Connect and RSPB Scotland proved that the team’s method can accurately assess forest expansion at a landscape scale. Airborne LiDAR has previously only been piloted for young-tree mapping, but this new study shows it can be used to survey millions of trees in 3D, and can accurately map natural woodland expansion. The team says its approach has potential to complement, or partially replace, hundreds of hours of work by staff and volunteers to physically survey sites on the ground - and could be used around the world to monitor forest management and restoration. A reversal of fortunes Scotland’s only native coniferous forests have suffered centuries of decline through tree clearance for agriculture and hunting. Only 4% of the original native forests now remain and the landscape is extensively heath, bogs and grassland. The study assessed land within the Cairngorms Connect partnership, the largest contiguous nature restoration partnership in the UK, which aims to double the size of the existing forest - largely through natural regeneration. This aligns with the Scottish Government’s long-term strategy to capture more carbon by creating 3,000-5,000 hectares of native woodland across Scotland each year. Until recently, deer browsing and the high cost of planting new trees within fenced areas has held back woodland expansion in Scotland. Now, a decade since the RSPB Scotland, Forestry and Land Scotland, NatureScot, and WildLand Ltd came together to form the Cairngorms Connect partnership, this study shows that over 5,235 hectares of previously open land supports young woodland - defined as land with over 100 trees per hectare. This has largely established naturally, with only small areas of planting where natural seed sources are not available. The ability to track the success of forest regeneration is vital for informing future land-management approaches. The Scottish Government is now funding a nationwide LiDAR survey, and the team is hopeful that its method will be used for monitoring nature recovery in Scotland and the rest of the UK. In addition to removing carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, more forested land is a boost for threatened species including Capercaillie and red squirrels, which are currently restricted to Scotland’s remaining forest fragments. This research was undertaken by Cambridge’s Centre for Landscape Regeneration, funded by the Natural Environment Research Council (NERC) and the Endangered Landscapes and Seascapes Programme, in collaboration with Cairngorms Connect and RSPB Scotland. Tarides SAS also supported the work. The data feeds into a wider University of Cambridge project called Tessera, an AI foundation model that has learnt patterns in data from European Space Agency satellites. Tessera makes it possible for non-experts to use satellite data to map changes in forests over time. Reference S.Thapa & A.Chan et al: ‘ Tracking and modelling native woodland expansion in the Scottish Highlands using LiDAR .’ Journal of Applied Ecology, Sept 2026. articles.title: ‘The eels were climbing out of the water to die’: why did every fish in this idyllic lake perish overnight?
articles.description: Furnace Brook in East Sussex was home to carp, tench, bream, roach and trout – and 15 trailer-loads had to be buried. The mystery led to a neighbouring farm, and a story of waste, pollution and dirty rivers that reveals a lot about Britain today When Alistair and Diane Gould bought Furnace Brook in 2013, they had big plans. It was an idyllic spot: a stream-fed fishing lake nestled in a secluded valley in the High Weald, East Sussex, surrounded by woodland and fields. “People loved to come fishing here because it’s so beautiful,” says Diane. “Some of them had been coming for so many years that they got to know the individual fish.” Diane moved here from Kent in 2000, when Furnace Brook was owned by a distant relative. Her two younger sons, then 10 and 14, flourished. They would chat to the anglers about the fish they were catching and throwing back in, and sell them bacon sandwiches. Her elder son, Simon, moved from London to join them in 2006 and became a keen angler himself, and then the fishing manager, or bailiff, looking after the fish and the landscape around the lake.
